reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: A primary bacterial infection of skeletal muscle that forms an intramuscular abscess, most often affecting large muscles such as the thigh, buttock, or trunk
Staphylococcus aureus, including community-acquired MRSA, is the leading cause
Classically described in tropical regions but increasingly recognised in temperate climates, especially in diabetics and immunocompromised or HIV-positive patients
Evolves through an early invasive phase of vague muscle ache and low-grade fever, a suppurative phase with abscess and localised signs, and a late septic phase
Early disease is easily missed because overlying skin often looks normal and superficial fluctuance is absent
MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting muscle inflammation and abscess formation
Management principles combine antistaphylococcal antibiotics with drainage of any abscess, either percutaneously or surgically
Blood cultures are frequently positive and multiple muscle sites can be involved, so a thorough search is warranted
reference.pathophysiology: Pyomyositis is a suppurative infection arising within skeletal muscle, thought to require transient bacteraemia together with muscle that has been rendered susceptible by trauma, strenuous exercise, or underlying compromise. Skeletal muscle is normally resistant to infection, but injury allows haematogenously seeded bacteria to establish a focus that progresses from diffuse inflammation to a walled-off intramuscular abscess. Without drainage the infection can extend, cause systemic sepsis, and, if untreated, seed distant sites.
additionalDifferentials: Deep vein thrombosis of the affected limb
Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of an adjacent bone
Necrotising fasciitis in the septic phase
infectionMimics: Deep vein thrombosis presenting with limb swelling and pain
additionalInvestigations: MRI to localise muscle inflammation and abscess; ultrasound or CT as alternatives
Aspiration or drainage of collected pus for Gram stain and culture
Creatine kinase, which is often only mildly elevated despite muscle involvement
Screening for diabetes, HIV, or other immunosuppression
redFlags: Signs of septic shock in the late phase requiring urgent resuscitation
Rapidly spreading pain and toxicity raising concern for necrotising fasciitis needing surgical exploration
Extension into adjacent joint or bone suggesting septic arthritis or osteomyelitis
Large or multiple abscesses requiring prompt drainage
reference.prognosis: With timely antibiotics and adequate drainage the outlook is generally good; delayed diagnosis, extensive or multifocal disease, and progression to septic shock worsen outcomes, and immunocompromised patients are at higher risk of complications.
pitfalls: Dismissing early muscle pain with normal-looking skin as a simple strain
Relying on creatine kinase, which may be near normal, to exclude the diagnosis
Treating with antibiotics alone when an abscess needs drainage
Failing to look for additional muscle foci or an underlying immunocompromising condition
